title: Ponticianus and Anthony (8.6)
hookLine: hearing of Anthony, Augustine is ashamed that the unlearned rise up
tomorrow: can you want something and not want it at the same time?

lines: NOT ALWAYS THE ONE WITH DEGREES.
cards: The person who sees most clearly what to do isn't always the one with the degrees. Sometimes it's the custodian, the grandmother, the kid who just does the kind thing. Augustine learns that at home in Milan.
A visitor named Ponticianus, a fellow African with a post at the emperor's court, spots a book on the game table, opens it, and finds the letters of Paul. He smiles.
Then he starts talking about a monk from the deserts of Egypt named Anthony, and two professors find out what a monk can teach them.

teach.b: First, Anthony. Ponticianus is amazed that Augustine and his friend Alypius have never heard of him. They also hadn't known about a monastery just outside the walls of Milan, under Ambrose's care.
Second, an afternoon at Trier. Ponticianus once went walking there with friends. Two of them wandered into a small house where some servants of God lived, and found a book: the life of Anthony.
One began to read, and before he finished he decided to leave his career at court and serve God. His friend joined him on the spot. Third, Augustine's face.
While Ponticianus talks, Augustine says, God was turning him around to look at himself, at the life he had kept behind his own back so he wouldn't have to see it. Fourth, the cry.
When the visitor leaves, he turns on Alypius. In his Latin: surgunt indocti et caelum rapiunt.
The unlearned rise up and take heaven by force, and here we are, with all our learning.
The shame isn't the end of him. It's the beginning of the turn.

how: Catholics read the lives of the saints, Anthony of Egypt among them, as examples to learn from, and the Church teaches that every baptized person, learned or not, is called to holiness.

o: a visitor's stories of a monk that shamed a professor
two scholars debating Paul's letters in Milan
a bishop's sermon on the deserts of Egypt

games.q: the visitor's stories — tap the pairs.
p: an African with a post at court

s: Augustine and Alypius already knew all about Anthony
Ponticianus was amazed they'd never heard of him.
the book Ponticianus found on the table was Paul's letters
he smiled to find it there.
Augustine's shame made him give up on changing
the shame was the beginning of the turn, not the end of him.

games.q: you're tutoring a younger kid in math, and you find out she visits her sick neighbor every day after school. what would Augustine's reaction to Anthony suggest?
o: let her goodness teach you something your learning hasn't.
keep it to math; how she lives isn't your subject.
teach her that real goodness needs good arguments.
games.why: Augustine, the professor, was shaken by people who simply did the thing. The unlearned rise up, he cried, and here we are with all our learning.

practice: Write by hand the name of someone who lives goodness more simply than you could explain it, and under the name, one thing they actually do. Then spend the sit just looking at those two lines.
If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Ponticianus and Anthony. A visitor's stories about a desert monk, and a professor ashamed that the unlearned rise first.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 8.8: the unlearned rise up and take heaven by force.

carryVoice: The unlearned rise, and sometimes the simplest life is the clearest teacher in the room. See you tomorrow.
